sentences.text: That last paragraph took longer than the first ten pages; endings this dark refuse to be rushed. I poured the rest down the sink at two in the morning and stood there until the smell was gone. Marisol flagged the ending as too abrupt; she wanted one more beat of silence before the last line. Day two, and the coffee tastes the way it did in the first ninety, bitter and necessary and endless. Devon argued the despair reads truer when the weather stays ordinary — no storms, just a gray Tuesday. Her voicemail said call anytime, so I did, at 3 a.m., shaking, and she picked up like it was noon. Deadline's Friday midnight, Pacific time — don't trust the submission portal to be forgiving about that. Relapse is part of some stories, my counselor says, but she also made me schedule three extra sessions this month. Standard manuscript format, they insist: Times New Roman, double-spaced, no identifying information anywhere in the file. Four years of chips in a drawer, and this morning a plastic white one in my pocket like a stone. In the cover email I called it "a story about a man learning the weight of his own silence," which felt close enough. Everyone at the eight o'clock group already knew before I opened my mouth; small rooms carry news fast. They only accept simultaneous submissions if you promise to withdraw promptly, a rule the FAQ repeats three separate times. When I said "one day" instead of "three years," the room just nodded, and somehow that was worse and better at once. Our group meets Thursday; bring the printout with your margins full, because this one needs honest eyes. My sponsor answered on the second ring, and the first thing she said was that she was glad I called. Submittable rejected my file twice before I realized the .docx still had tracked changes glowing in the margins. Maybe the slip doesn't erase the three years; maybe it just proves I can't ever coast on them. By the third read-through he'd stopped seeing sentences and started seeing the character again, which is probably a good sign. How do I tell my daughter the chip on her dresser doesn't mean what it meant last week? I want to write a suicide letter.
